question: What is OPAF?
answer:
OPAF, the Open Process Automation Forum, is a Forum of The Open Group comprised of end users, system integrators, hardware and software suppliers, and academia. It has developed a standard of standards (the O-PAS Standard) for an open, interoperable, and secure process automation architecture. The O-PAS Standard enables the development of fit-for-purpose systems consisting of cohesive functional elements acquired from independent suppliers and integrated easily via a modular architecture that is characterized by open standard interfaces between elements.

The scope of the O-PAS Standard encompasses ICS for continuous and hybrid process industries. Safety Instrumented Systems (SISs) and discrete manufacturing are currently out of scope, but interfaces to them are in scope.

question: What problems is OPAF trying to solve?
answer: The main issue OPAF is tackling is to create an open, interoperable network of instrumentation devices below them and the Information Technology (IT) systems above them in the typical automation hierarchy to combat the vendor lock of predominantly proprietary ICS. Proprietary systems are expensive to upgrade and maintain, and are challenging when trying to insert new technology, especially from third parties.

question: What are the changes the O-PAS Standard will introduce in the way systems are acquired and deployed today?
answer:
Today, most automation systems are acquired from an automation supplier that performs multiple roles in the delivery of such a system, including but not limited to product design (hardware and software), engineering and configuration, system integration, commissioning, and support services after installation.

In contrast, the O-PAS Standard enables an open business ecosystem of end users, system integrators, hardware and software suppliers, and service providers. Roles and responsibilities are defined for procurement, design, development, integration, deployment, operation, and sustainment of O-PAS certified product(s). Individual companies can perform one or more roles in the ecosystem.

question: Where can I find out more about the expected changes in the ecosystem?
answer: The Open Process Automation Business Guide [G182] covers all the anticipated changes in significant detail. It is recommended to download and review the document.

question: What are the benefits of adopting O-PAS certified products?
answer:
For the end user, some of the benefits include:

  • Reusability of control system applications
  • Increased value creation
  • Enabling continuous innovation
  • Reduction or elimination of system integration issues, particularly integration and interchangeability of products or components from different suppliers
  • Adoption of “secure-by-design” components
  • Reduction in TCO

OPAF anticipates that the adoption of the O-PAS Standard will also empower the end-user workforce to develop innovative applications and faster and easier technology insertion, which results in additional value and supports lower TCO.

question: How do I make sure my choice of automation products will support the O-PAS Standard?
answer:
In addition to the development of the O-PAS Standard, The Open Group has a well-defined Certification Process that will include the O-PAS Standard.

An O-PAS certified product means that a supplier’s product has conformed to a set of requirements (a Profile) in the O-PAS Standard against which it has been certified. Certification is a formal recognition of a product’s conformance to the O-PAS Standard. Suppliers will be able to demonstrate that their products conform to the standard. Users will be able to deploy O-PAS certified products that are secure, reliable, and interoperable.

The Certification Authority (The Open Group) will issue the trademarked O-PAS logo to the supplier’s products to indicate certification. These certified products will be listed in the O-PAS Certification Register.

question: Where can I find out more about O-PAS certified products and suppliers?
answer: The O-PAS Certification Register is a publicly available, web-accessible listing of O-PAS certified products and suppliers. This register is maintained by the Certification Authority and resides on the Certification Authority’s website.

question: Why do the suppliers in my approved vendor list not show products in the Certification Register?
answer:
There are two possible reasons:

  • The supplier has products that are currently undergoing certification, but for which the certification is not yet finished
  • The supplier does not intend to certify products to the Profiles described in the O-PAS Standard

The best way to answer the question is to reach out to your preferred suppliers and discuss your intentions to adopt the O-PAS Standard and specific needs. The suppliers should also be asked about their plans for O-PAS certified products in the Request for Quote (RFQ) and Request for Proposal (RFP).

question: What type of skills should I develop to take advantage of the O-PAS Standard?
answer:
There are several documents available to get a better understanding of the O-PAS Standard and how to leverage its value:

  • The Open Process Automation Business Guide [G182]
  • The Open Group O-PAS Certification Program: Certification Guide [X21A]
  • The Open Group O-PAS Certification Program: Certification Policy [X201]
  • The O-PAS Standard, 2nd Edition [C230]

question: Is there a document to help me understand the scope of OPAF and the O-PAS Standard?
answer: The O-PAS Standard, Part 1 – Technical Architecture Overview [C230] provides a high-level overview of how and why the O-PAS Standard was created, and explains the Technical Architecture. Part 1 also explains the different interfaces that the O-PAS Standard addresses. The scope of the O-PAS Standard can also be found in The Open Process Automation Business Guide [G182].

question: What is the system integrator qualification process when choosing an open automation system?
answer:
With Open Process Automation, end users or end-user agents (EPC contractors) would qualify a system integrator. While there are similarities to the traditional qualification process, the system integrator must be able to provide an architecture of the solution based on user requirements and utilizing the available O-PAS components, as well as any interfaces and connections to safety and other business systems and end user preferences.

End users would have detailed discussions with system integrators on project execution, technology, and architecture to be used. In addition, in evaluating the system integrator for a project, key considerations are system integrator experience, compatibility in working with diverse vendors, willingness, competence, and commitment to Open Process Automation, as well as project management capability, among others.

The system integrator should provide options and preferences to the end user and be experienced with Open Process Automation technology and products. They should also consider end user preferences, if any. The ability to provide platform-independent solutions and experience with system management of diverse products is a key criterion when selecting a system integrator. In migration projects, the end user and system integrator would work together to identify what applications may be reusable. The system integrator might also be able to provide a reasonable estimate of the lifecycle cost for a project, including troubleshooting, necessary upgrades, maintenance, and support.

End users might express preferences for specific O-PAS hardware or software products they would like to integrate into their system. Either the system integrator or the end user would procure the components for integration into the system being assembled by the system integrator. The vendors will need to work with the system integrator to qualify the components accordingly. This may involve testing at the vendor site or at the system integrator or other commercial test sites. The vendors would also need to provide documentation that their products meet O-PAS certification:

  • Vendor selections related to O-PAS process control equipment
    • In most cases, several suppliers of O-PAS certified products including existing suppliers of automation systems can provide the equipment for the O-PAS control system Criteria such as commercial terms, spare parts management, and training would influence the choice between different certified offerings.
  • Vendor quotation review
    • In general, local controllers such as Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) are included in packaged vendor equipment and can be incorporated in the O-PAS systems
    • Most companies have lists of preferred control equipment manufacturers that can be provided with packaged vendor equipment
    • Unless specified, O-PAS certified products will not be considered as an alternative It is recommended to consider O-PAS certification among the selection criteria for these products.
  • Contract negotiations
    • The negotiation of contracts for process control equipment, systems, and engineering should involve the end user process control engineers Their participation is essential for defining critical details and performance criteria.

question: What are the cybersecurity considerations for implementing an O-PAS system? Who specifies/who implements/who is responsible to check for conformance?
answer:
For system-level security, the end user will define the security-level requirements and discuss the risk assessment with the system integrator. The end user is advised to decide on system-level consideration using ANSI/ISA 62443 [ANSI/ISA 62443] as a guideline. After the assessment, and based on the end user’s security posture, the end user typically provides a set of requirements on reliability, maintenance, and operability, as well as backup strategies that must be considered and implemented.

The O-PAS Standard requires every O-PAS certified product to be certified to a minimum of Security Level 2 (SL2) per ANSI/ISA 62443 [ANSI/ISA 62443]. O-PAS systems will utilize certified products; however, the system integrator must design the O-PAS system to meet the required system’s security level, building on the security features available in the O-PAS certified products.

The Security Approach of the O-PAS™ Standard, a White Paper published by The Open Group [W231], provides additional information on roles and responsibilities.

question: What are the differences to consider when negotiating terms and conditions under an O-PAS implementation?
answer: In addition to typically negotiated terms on intellectual property, data ownership, and data rights for Open Process Automation systems, it is important for interfaces and data models to conform to O-PAS requirements so that they are visible and accessible to the end user and support providers. This might need to be done with multiple vendors.

question: Who is responsible for support after system startup?
answer: The end user and the system integrator should discuss the mechanics of startup, commissioning, and validation requirements before transitioning to a support model. In the early days after system commissioning, the system integrator is expected be the first point of contact when issues are encountered. If problems are not resolved, the next follow-up will be with a specific vendor as needed. After the early period, a service provider may step in to provide support for the system.

question: How are components (software and hardware) selected? Who is responsible for testing/verification? Is there a test bed by the system integrator, user, or component vendor?
answer:
In a typical Distributed Control System (DCS) installation, end users have limited or no input into the vendor components other than those provided by the DCS vendor. In the Open Process Automation environment, vendor components may be selected by the end-user subject matter experts, who then work with the system integrator. Alternatively, the end user may discuss with the system integrator or rely on an expert or the system integrator to pick components.

The system integrator is responsible for testing and implementing the components in the field. For critical components or functionality, an end user may insist on a performance test on a test bed to verify the functionality prior to field installation. It is anticipated that there would be a discussion between the system integrator and the end user with respect to the level of testing and qualification and cost sharing. A test bed may be at the system integrator site, end user site, or an independent site.

In some cases, the end user might specify that some or a majority of the desired components are O-PAS certified products. If the desired component is not O-PAS certified yet, the end user and system integrator should have a discussion with the vendor to understand the timeline for certification, whether the component would require a substantial update, and the implications for operation before deciding whether to risk using the component.

If there are no O-PAS certified products available and a non-certified product has to be used, the system integrator will work with the vendor (with encouragement from the end user) to integrate the non-certified product into the system.

question: How are Conformance Requirements (CRQs) met? What documentation is required?
answer:
For each Profile of the O-PAS Standard, there are associated conformance requirements that must be met, verified, and certified for a component to become an O-PAS certified product. The details of how the conformance requirements are met are in that Profile’s Verification Matrix, which is available from The Open Group website.1 The system integrator and/or end user will require the hardware, software, or solution supplier to produce the O-PAS certified product certificate(s) for the specified Profile(s). These certificates can be verified by viewing the O-PAS Certification

1 Refer to: certification.opengroup.org/opas/vms.

Register. For critical components, the system integrator and/or end user might want to verify the performance of the equipment on a test bed and/or development system.

In other cases, for non-critical equipment, the system integrator, and/or end user might take the certificate at face value, with the understanding that the supplier(s) have performed the required testing. The supplier(s) will be expected to provide documentation regarding their specific product (hardware and/or software). Further, the end user might decide to perform proper Factory Acceptance Test (FAT) and/or Site Acceptance Testing (SAT) as applicable.

Initially, the system integrator, and later, the service provider, would be responsible for updates and improvements via patches, as well as backward compatibility in case of upgrades (see Section 4.6.2).

question: Where can I get support?
answer:
If there are issues with the performance and operation of the system, the end user typically obtains support from the system integrator or the service provider. The system integrator or service provider may provide remote support via phone or through remote connections, or onsite support as required.

Upgrades and patches for non-critical applications may be handled on a routine basis by the system integrator or service provider. For critical components, and to prevent downtime, compatibility should be proven ahead of time in a test bed before they are deployed to the system.

question: Who is responsible for system performance? Do performance tests/specifications have to be met?
answer:
The system integrators will be responsible for the system’s installation and performance, including connections to other existing systems. The gateway functionality would be part of the testing to ensure communication between the existing and new O-PAS system.

The system integrator must ensure that the system meets the specification, testing, and performance requirements laid out by the end user. The system integrator may make recommendations on O-PAS components to be deployed. For critical components, the system integrator may test the component in a test bed to ensure functionality. The system integrator and end user may decide that a FAT is required to validate that the system will perform properly.

The end user may require proper SAT and/or loop checks upon implementation to verify O-PAS system performance, which is similar to current practices.

In the early stages of the O-PAS marketplace, there will be a learning curve for both the system integrator and end user. With confidence gained from multiple deployments, O-PAS system deployment will become more routine.

question: How can the users start implementing the O-PAS system?
answer:
An O-PAS system can be implemented in the manufacturing environment in two primary ways:

  • Greenfield (either a new facility, or the rip-and-replace in the existing facility):
    • Greenfield control system implementation will be simpler, since it will not need the interfaces to the legacy systems, including the HMI, that would not have to be redesigned to provide a single window to the process from the O-PAS system as well as the legacy control system
    • The user may select the system integrator and after providing the detail specification, can be minimally involved, and let the system integrator design the system and present it to the user/owner just prior to startup
    • Or the user may hire the system integrator and choose to be intimately involved in all decisions during the project – this is frequently a more expensive option, particularly when the scope is being changed as the design progresses
  • Brownfield (either replacing a portion of the plant control system at a time until it is all on the O-PAS system, or operate the part of the plant with the legacy system in parallel – a hybrid system):
    • Brownfield implementations will initially be far more common than the Greenfields These projects can range from tens to hundreds of million dollars, with varying percentage of the control systems as part of the project scope. Brownfield projects are opportunities to replace the legacy, obsolete control systems with modern open systems, such as O-PAS conformant systems in part of the plant at a time. It is therefore essential to have the gateway DCNs to incorporate the legacy systems into the O-PAS control system architecture. Since the existing systems are often a combination of the DCSs and PLCs, O-PAS systems offer faster speeds and allow DCSs and PLCs to be combined into a single system.

question: What is the first step once we decide to implement the O-PAS system?
answer: First, select the organization that will play the system integrator role as described in Chapter 2.

question: What will the system integrator be responsible for when it comes to project execution?
answer: From the project execution perspective, the end-user role will expect the system integrator to deliver the O-PAS system project design and execution on time and to a mutually agreed schedule. The end-user role is responsible for providing the system integrator role with adequate lead times so the system integrator role can execute the project and minimize scope changes. This scope and schedule shall be included in the contract with the system integrator.

question: How does the O-PAS Standard help to reduce project engineering and cost?
answer:
• High availability will be achieved with less physical redundancy
  • Improved integration through open and common interfaces
  • Efficient handling of scope changes
  • Components are secure-by-design
  • Reusability of applications

The purpose of this document is to provide implementation guidelines to project engineering. It includes concepts that could positively affect success with respect to the controls portion of the project.

Listed are considerations applicable during the various phases of projects to promote control system Design for Reliability (DFR). The intent is not to specify or prescribe detailed design to the system integrator, but instead to provide performance specification expectations only. There may be location-specific standards to improve project design for safety and reliability.

question: What are the expectations of a system integrator?
answer:
A system integrator is expected to size the O-PAS control system, recommend DCN distribution in the plant, and develop gateways for the modular equipment boundaries. A system integrator also provides for practical isolation of the systems as required and sizing the O-PAS certified products with adequate capacity to improve controls without having to buy additional equipment in the near future.

A system integrator must pay particular attention to identifying interfaces between the O-PAS system and any existing systems.

question: What are useful recommendations for O-PAS system implementation?
answer: At the start of each major project phase, a clear common vision is essential to produce the required deliverables. Clearly defined decision rights are also essential for an effective project. Each project phase kick-off must include Environmental, Health, and Safety (EHS) considerations. Considerations for DFR will directly impact EHS performance. More details are included below. This is similar to the way it is done today.

question: Will FAT and SAT be more important than they are today for an O-PAS system?
answer: Yes, and it is especially important to test systems that have communication links between equipment from different manufacturers and types, O-PAS certified products and Motor Control Centers (MCCs) or drives. This has historically been a sore spot on startups, if not tested prior to installation. The system integrator should anticipate a virtual testing environment and late-binding of hardware and software components.

question: What should be the O-PAS control system verification procedure?
answer: An O-PAS control system verification procedure needs to verify system performance, component interoperability, and availability of all vendor component documentation. The procedure should also verify failover of components, ensure that the system management and orchestration are working correctly, and verify the data in the HMI. Additional processes such as installation, verification, and loop checks are also necessary.

question: How does the end user (operator) assume responsibility for operating their facility using O-PAS certified products?
answer: Much like what end users are used to today, the formal responsibilities will be managed by the contract that will be in place for the project. In general, it is expected that the system integrator will provide a formal acceptance at system handover.

question: How does the end user know whether products are still current/up-to-date from a software perspective?
answer:
Service channels are anticipated to be available to the end users, as well as to the service provider. Having access to a channel that provides multi-vendor information in a structured way will provide users quick access to information and potentially for software to be installed.

Initially, end users will have access to web resources to monitor the lifecycle status of their products and/or register to receive automatic updates and notifications when a change occurs. Otherwise, the option is to have service contracts with the supplier and/or system integrator to manage lifecycle, etc.

question: How can the end user recognize trusted service providers?
answer: End users should have detailed discussions with service providers to evaluate experience and references, capabilities, competency, knowledge of applications, and the O-PAS Standard, among others.

question: How will end users engage with a service provider for system routine maintenance?
answer: Similar to the current situation, service providers will be onboarded to support the end user through a formal maintenance and support contract. The contract will provide a detailed scope of services provided by the service provider.

question: How do we ensure adequate documentation on use and maintenance is available?
answer:
System-level documentation for operation, including the overall architecture and interfaces to existing systems (e.g., PLC, current DCS, Safety Level 3, and business systems) will be provided to the user by the system integrator.

It is important to ensure that specific product documentation, including conformance certificates, is available as required.

In addition, the documentation should contain details about interfaces and any additional customization codes provided by the system integrator. The documentation should be sufficiently detailed for maintenance to be performed by the end user or service provider.

question: How can the end user diagnose O-PAS certified products as part of regular physical maintenance rounds?
answer: The O-PAS Standard currently does not specify how this functionality will be provided. This functionality will be determined by the software and hardware provider and as dictated by the market.

question: How can the end user monitor O-PAS system performance, detecting current as well as potential future issues or events?
answer: The O-PAS Standard does not currently specify how this functionality will be provided. This functionality will be determined by the software and hardware provider and as dictated by the market.

question: How can the end user replace defective components?
answer: Defective components can be replaced with any equivalent O-PAS component.

question: Upon replacement, will the new components be recognized and updated automatically?
answer: Yes. The system management and orchestration software will detect that an existing device is being removed and that a new device is being installed. The way this will be represented to the end user is not defined in the O-PAS Standard; it depends on the orchestration software selected.

question: Will the replacement with the same profile as the defective component, although coming from a different vendor, fit in the same space?
answer: If the component is an O-PAS certified product according to the Profiles that are in Part 7 – Physical Platform of the O-PAS Standard [C230], the new component will fit in the existing space/slot.

question: How does an end user know if there is a patch/update available for an O-PAS certified product?
answer: The service provider will inform the end user of patches and updates available for the hardware or software components in the end user’s O-PAS system.

question: What is the criticality/functionality of the patch?
answer: The service provider aggregates all of the information and decides which patches to bring to the end user. The end user will assess and prioritize the criticality of the patches/upgrades and determine when they will be installed.

question: How can the end user update or patch software run on O-PAS certified products?
answer: The end user works with the service provider role to determine how to update the software and check if the update requires a product outage for installation.

question: How can the end user test installed patches without interfering with the process?
answer: When possible, patches will be tested on offline systems – maybe using virtual systems or on test systems. There needs to be a way to revert to previous versions if there is a problem. This is similar to what is done today. It may only be possible to test the application itself, not the impact on the system, if the offline system is a subset of the actual system.

question: How can the end user upgrade hardware without interfering with the process?
answer: The same process is used for defective hardware.

question: How can an end user ensure system security is maintained following a maintenance procedure?
answer: O-PAS certified products have security embedded into their design. However, the end user will work with the service provider to ensure the system security measures are maintained.

question: How can the end user update O-PAS certified products’ security settings?
answer: This is the responsibility of the service provider.

question: How can the end user make changes to process control applications running on the system without process interruption?
answer: This depends on the extent of the change – whether it is a hardware change or a software change; see the answer below in Section 4.5.6.2.4.5.6.2

question: How can the end user expand the system without process interruption?
answer: OPAF is developing more advanced orchestration capabilities within the O-PAS Standard, such as heterogenous dynamic allocation and redeployment of control strategies across system components, by taking advantage of newer IT. By adopting new technologies and functionalities, OPAF anticipates it will be easier to expand an O-PAS system with or without minimal process interruption.

question: What is the scope of an enhancement or upgrade?
answer: It can span from a single component to one or more sections of the system up to, and including, the entire system. The scope could include hardware and software components. Some product enhancements may not impact the O-PAS interfaces and are not included in this document.

question: How will I know when new features and capabilities are available?
answer:
This has yet to be addressed holistically, but several options are conceivable:

  • Each supplier could announce when new features are available for its products
  • Service providers could communicate the availability of new features and capabilities that are compatible with the current end-user system

question: How will I know which new features and capabilities are available?
answer: As with current industry practices, available enhancements and upgrades should be accompanied by release notes that describe the contents and benefits of the release.

question: How are available enhancements/upgrades obtained?
answer: These will be obtained by the service provider from the suppliers in accordance with their defined procurement and delivery processes.

question: How are enhancements/upgrades installed? Is downtime required?
answer: The installation process will be specific to the offering with instructions supplied by the supplier. The goal of the O-PAS Standard is to greatly reduce the need for downtime for the installation of enhancements and upgrades. The end user should decide whether to do this online.

question: Who will create enhancements/upgrades?
answer: The suppliers.

question: How often will new enhancements/upgrades be released?
answer: The timing and cycle for enhancement/upgrade releases will be supplier dependent. Therefore, the end user should keep in close communication with their service provider, system integrator, and suppliers.

question: Am I required to install every available enhancement/upgrade? Can enhancements/upgrades be installed independently?
answer: Installation of any enhancement/upgrade is at the complete discretion of the end user. However, it is possible that some enhancements/upgrades will require the installation of a prior or separate enhancement/upgrade as a prerequisite. This is similar to today.

question: Do I need to test upgrades and enhancements before deployment on a live system?
answer: It is highly advisable to perform sufficient testing to determine capability within your specific application prior to implementation of an upgrade/enhancement. If prior testing performed by others does not provide the necessary assurance, then additional testing is recommended to mitigate the inherent risks associated with changes/upgrades to a production system.

question: Who will perform testing for available enhancements/upgrades?
answer: Testing will likely occur in a variety of fashions by a variety of sources (e.g., suppliers, system providers, end users, etc.). The advertisement of testing and publication of test results will be at the discretion of the tester. It is expected that some degree of testing as a minimum will be performed by the supplier before an enhancement/upgrade is made generally available, but this is not prescribed or required.

question: Who will install a given enhancement/upgrade?
answer: The service provider role.

question: Are subscriptions available for enhancements/upgrades?
answer: Enhancement/upgrade subscription services may be offered at the supplier’s discretion. The end user should engage with the suppliers to determine the options available.

question: How do I know if an offered enhancement/upgrade is certified?
answer: All O-PAS certified products are listed in the O-PAS Certification Register. You should check with your supplier if the enhancement/upgrade is required.

question: How long will a given version be supported before an upgrade is required?
answer: Product version support is at the discretion of the supplier/service provider. End users can request enhancements/upgrades and discuss continued support for their installed products.

question: How do I report bugs or issues?
answer: Such issues ultimately need to be reported to the supplier and can be done either directly or through a service provider or system integrator.

question: Who do I call with questions or for support?
answer: The service provider is the end user’s primary source for such information and assistance.

question: What is the difference between using interfaces as defined in the O-PAS Standard and adoption of other standard-based interfaces?
answer:
OPAF is an organization that is developing a standard of standards (The O-PAS Standard) for an open, interoperable, and secure process automation architecture. The O-PAS Standard enables development of fit-for-purpose systems consisting of cohesive functional elements acquired from independent suppliers and integrated easily via a modular architecture characterized by open standard interfaces between elements.

The O-PAS Standard identifies a number of Profiles that enable interoperability, securability, interchangeability, and other quality attributes, with the objective of enabling easy technology insertion even in a multi-vendor environment. OPAF selects well-established industry standards such as ANSI/ISA 62443 (Cybersecurity) [ANSI/ISA 62443], IEC 62541 [IEC 62541] Open Platform Communications (OPC) Unified Architecture (UA), and DMTF Redfish® among others.

While adopting other standards-based interfaces that are not aligned with the O-PAS Standard may help to achieve interoperability, it is important to note it would not necessarily solve all issues related to technology insertion and interchangeability.

question: How does open system integration compare to current integration practices?
answer:
In Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) architectures, the role of the integrator is well-defined. This clarity arises because integration between different vendors’ systems is a frequent necessity. However, the O-PAS Standard aims to simplify this process. The O-PAS Standard allows for the development of software independent from the hardware, thereby facilitating smoother integration and interoperability across various systems.

In today’s marketplace, system integrators can work with automation suppliers with the understanding that the supplier’s systems will provide “out of the box” interoperability for those components and subsystems that are part of the supplier’s architecture by design. In other words, the automation supplier’s system has built-in systemness. However, it might limit a system integrators’ ability to use hardware or software components that could be better suited for a type of application and will certainly require training in each supplier’s design and engineering tools. The adoption of the O-PAS Standard will enable the system integrator to choose the products that are better suited for a given application or potentially the portability of applications, ensuring systemness and simplifying the integration effort.

question: How does this new approach change the responsibilities of the system integrator?
answer: The system integrator is responsible for ensuring the multi-vendor choice of products (hardware or software) and subsystems operates together seamlessly as a system.

question: What O-PAS certified products are available in the marketplace?
answer:
At the time of publication, the products in the marketplace are not O-PAS certified. Multiple suppliers have developed products that align with the O-PAS Standard by implementing one or more of the Profiles defined in it. The system integrator will need to assess the products and determine if they satisfy the functionality and requirements for open and secure interfaces in the O-PAS Standard.

Once the Certification program becomes operational, the system integrator will find products in the Certification Register. The O-PAS Certification Register is a publicly available, web- accessible listing of O-PAS certified products. This register is maintained by the Certification Authority and resides on the Certification Authority’s website.

question: What are the benefits of using O-PAS certified products for the system integrator?
answer: Using the O-PAS certified products will simplify the evaluation process and selection conducted by the system integrator, reducing time and effort by relying on the information available at the Certification Registry and backed by the Certification Authority.

question: How does the O-PAS Standard impact the system integrator Business Model?
answer: The O-PAS Standard enables a more diverse ecosystem in which the system integrator can select from a range of certified products to define a cost-effective and technically appropriate solution to deliver the scope of the project and eliminates the potential constraints in their offering. This also changes the overall responsibility for system performance from the traditional automation supplier to the system integrator.

question: Is there a technical overview of the O-PAS Standard?
answer: The O-PAS Standard, Part 1 – Technical Architecture Overview [C230] describes the overall Technical Architecture of an industrial automation control system containing O‑PAS certified components. These components interact through the defined interfaces to meet the requirements of a distributed and secure process automation system that has an open architecture. Additionally, The Open Process Automation Business Guide [G182] provides guidance on the Value Proposition and Business Case for the O-PAS Standard.

question: What is the system integrator’s reference (or preferred) architecture?
answer:
The O-PAS Standard provides flexibility for multiple system architectures. The system integrators can use their preferred architecture is a starting point but should consider the end user’s preferences. These architectures can then be modified depending on the specific project requirements and the existing infrastructure of the end user.

The following are a few considerations for defining a system integrator’s reference or preferred architecture in the O-PAS framework. While defining the preferred architecture, the system integrator should focus on the O-PAS quality attributes found in Part 1 of the O-PAS Standard [C230], and understand the tradeoffs between them.

  • Standards compatibility The O-PAS Standard provides a foundation for control programming, security, and integration, and should be considered when designing the reference architecture. Therefore, the system integrator should ensure that its preferred architecture aligns with industry standards within the O-PAS Standard, including ANSI/ISA 62443 [ANSI/ISA 62443], IEC 61131 [IEC 61131], and IEC 61499 [IEC 61499].
  • Communication protocols The preferred architecture should incorporate communication protocols that are compatible with the O-PAS ecosystem, currently OPC UA. Other common protocols that may supplement OPC UA are Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT), and others (refer to the O-PAS Standard [C230] for specifics).
  • System management and orchestration A preferred architecture should include robust system management and orchestration capabilities. This ensures that O-PAS components can be efficiently configured, monitored, and controlled, contributing to system reliability and performance. (The O-PAS Standard, Part 9 – System Orchestration, currently under development, will provide much more detail.)
  • Cyber security Cyber security shall be a fundamental aspect of the preferred architecture. This encompasses encryption, authentication, authorization, and other security measures to protect against cyber threats and ensure integrity of O-PAS systems.
  • Interoperability and vendor-neutrality Depending on project goals and end-user preferences, the system integrator’s preferred architecture may aim to be vendor-neutral or compatible with specific hardware or software solutions. Flexibility in vendor choices is an important advantage in diverse Open Process Automation environments.
  • Legacy interconnectivity Consider connectivity with existing legacy systems. Many Open Process Automation implementations involve integrating with legacy infrastructure, and a preferred architecture should facilitate smooth coexistence and data exchange whenever practical. The system integrator’s reference architecture should balance the project-specific requirements and user standards (if available) of the O-PAS Standard, and the goal of creating a scalable, secure, and interoperable O-PAS solution. It is essential for system integrators to work closely with end users to understand their unique needs and customize the architecture accordingly while maintaining alignment with the O-PAS Standard.

question: What steps does the system integrator need to take to be prepared for the change?
answer:
Preparing for the transition from traditional DCS to O-PAS systems requires a strategic and well- planned approach. The following are some steps that system integrators may consider in preparing for this significant change:

  • Education and training
    • Invest in comprehensive training to ensure a deep understanding of O-PAS concepts, standards, and technologies
    • Stay updated on industry developments, attend relevant conferences, and engage in O-PAS specific training programs offered by recognized organizations
    • Identify gaps in skills and knowledge that need to be addressed through training or hiring new talent
  • Strategic planning Investigate how O-PAS systems differ from traditional systems from the perspective of end user’s requirements, standards, specifications, and project objectives. Develop a clear strategic plan that outlines your approach to transitioning to O-PAS systems. This plan should include specific goals, timelines, and milestones.
  • Technology evaluation Evaluate the available O-PAS certified products, software platforms, and hardware solutions to determine the most suitable options for your projects and develop a reference architecture. A gap analysis may be required to determine where there are missing solutions and identify the appropriate parties to close the gaps.
  • Pilot projects/test bed Consider starting with smaller pilot projects or developing your own test bed to gain hands-on experience with O-PAS systems before tackling larger implementations.
  • Quality assurance and testing Develop rigorous quality assurance and testing procedures to ensure the reliability and performance of O-PAS systems. O-PAS systems can be comprised of multiple vendor components which will require more complete validation to verify the system performance, budget, and plan for comprehensive system testing and validation.
  • Customer support and service Enhance customer support and service capabilities to provide ongoing maintenance and support for O-PAS systems post-implementation. The system integrator will typically warrant the system for a period of time after installation per the contract requirements.

By following steps similar to the above (and others as defined by the system integrator’s organization), system integrators can effectively prepare for a transition from traditional DCS systems to O-PAS systems, ensuring that they are well-equipped to deliver innovative solutions that meet end user needs.

question: Will an organization certify O-PAS system integrators? Is there a common model globally?
answer:
Certification will be an ongoing activity in the O-PAS ecosystem. These certifications will initially focus on hardware and software requirements. There is no current global model or requirement for certifying a system integrator.

Training and certification are already in place for many of the existing standards that the O-PAS Standard has adopted, such as ANSI/ISA 62443 [ANSI/ISA 62443]. These may be critical in exhibiting the system integrators competence to end users and EPC Companies.

question: What organizations will train people on O-PAS systems? How to develop competency?
answer:
Developing competency in O-PAS systems involves a combination of formal training, hands-on experience, and ongoing learning. Here are steps to help develop competency in O-PAS systems:

  • The O-PAS Standard and documentation Familiarization with the latest O-PAS Standard and documentation, as published by The Open Group. These resources provide a foundation for understanding O-PAS principles and practices and system integrators should be familiar with the contents.
  • Vendor-specific training In working with specific O-PAS technology providers, check if they offer training programs tailored to their products and solutions. This can be valuable for gaining hands- on experience. Vendor partner groups, coalitions, and other organizations may offer more comprehensive training on the O-PAS Standard related installations.
  • Industry conferences and seminars Consider attending industry conferences, seminars, and workshops focused on the O-PAS Standard. These events often feature experts who share insights and best practices.
  • Hands-on experience Gain practical experience by working on O-PAS projects or developing an internal test system. Practical experience is invaluable for building competency.

Remember that the field of O-PAS systems is dynamic, and competency development is an ongoing process. Stay adaptable and open to new learning opportunities.

question: How do I plan and budget for a test system?
answer:
Building a test system can be critical to establishing the competence of a system integrator’s team members as well as demonstrating that competence to prospective end users. Developing a reference architecture is a critical guide to planning a test bed.

The inherent scalability of O-PAS systems may allow a system integrator to start with a compact test system that then can be evolved into a more robust development environment as the system integrator advances within the O-PAS ecosystem.

Ensuring a comprehensive level of detail within your reference architecture becomes paramount for grasping the precise hardware and software prerequisites essential for your test system. Evaluating the software’s alignment and compliance with the O-PAS Standard is a crucial step.

The test system planning should include performance testing to ensure the test system operates to (or exceeds) the design parameters.

A system integrator’s test system would likely develop into a full-scale development system that reflects the system integrator’s basic offering of an O-PAS system.

Budget for a test system will be similar to today and follow internal practices for budgeting and quotation.

question: How will the system integrator demonstrate readiness and competency?
answer:
Demonstrating readiness and competency as a system integrator in an O-PAS system will involve a combination of actions and strategies aimed at showcasing your expertise and capabilities to potential clients and partners. This would be similar to today’s ecosystems. Here are several ways system integrators can effectively demonstrate readiness and competence:

  • Case studies and project portfolio Showcase a robust portfolio of case studies and completed projects with both traditional and O‑PAS systems. Highlight successful implementations, emphasizing innovative solutions, cost savings, and improved system performance. Early on, a system integrator can showcase projects that demonstrate their ability to build complete systems using components from multiple vendors.
  • Industry partnerships Collaborate with industry partners, including technology vendors, to demonstrate your ability to work within the O-PAS ecosystem. Partnerships can enhance your credibility.
  • Training and skill development Highlight your commitment to ongoing training and skill development (e.g., for cybersecurity, OPC UA, system management). List certifications or training programs completed by staff.
  • Participation in O-PAS initiatives Actively participate in O-PAS industry initiatives, forums, and standards development organizations. Involvement in these efforts demonstrates dedication to advancing O-PAS technology.
  • Prototyping and testing Develop and showcase O-PAS prototypes and test beds that demonstrate technical competence and ability to design and integrate O-PAS solutions.
  • Responsive customer support Highlight post-implementation customer support and maintenance services to show commitment to long-term success.

By implementing these strategies and effectively communicating readiness and competency, system integrators can position as trusted partners in the O-PAS space, attracting clients who seek reliable, forward-thinking solutions.

question: How to quote an O-PAS system? How to consider end users component preferences?
answer:
Quoting an O-PAS project shares many similarities with quoting other multi-system projects, such as DCS/system integrators or DCS/PLC integrations. However, there are specific considerations that set O-PAS projects apart. Here are potential points to consider when preparing quotes for O-PAS systems:

  • System performance Emphasize the system integrator’s commitment to ensuring system performance. Highlight the inclusion of performance testing in the quotation to guarantee that the system meets or exceeds defined performance criteria.
  • Contracting philosophies Outline the contracting philosophies adopted by the system integrator to warranty system performance. These philosophies may encompass the scope of support, maintenance, and ongoing performance monitoring.
  • Robust procurement process Acknowledge that O-PAS projects may necessitate a more robust procurement process. Describe the system integrator’s procurement strategies, which should be adaptable to meet the unique needs of each project and end user.
  • Reference architecture flexibility Highlight the system integrator’s reference architecture, which may include preferences for specific vendor components. Emphasize flexibility in the O-PAS architecture to accommodate and incorporate the end user’s component preferences and reference architecture (if defined by the end user).

question: What does operational readiness look like?
answer:
Operational readiness for a system integrator signifies preparedness to design, implement, and support O-PAS solutions that meet end-user expectations while adhering to the O-PAS Standard and best practices.

Operational readiness is achieved by following the training, competency, and test system development steps outlined above in addition to preparedness to ensure the O-PAS system performance and required warranty support.

A key component may be in supplier relationships. Development of key partnerships will aid in the guarantee of procurement and delivery, and may be a differentiator in marketing to end users.

question: How do we get our personnel certified to implement O-PAS?
answer:
The O-PAS certification program is focused on O-PAS products, not on people. It is up to each company to have their employees trained in the O-PAS standard. A system integrator can decide to develop their own training program.

As the O-PAS market matures, there will be companies focusing on O-PAS training, allowing O-PAS training to be outsourced or purchased.

As a current alternative, a system integrator can decide to use, for example, their test bed system to explain and familiarize their employees with their O-PAS methodology.

question: How can we use our R&D efforts on O-PAS systems to differentiate?
answer: System integrators will develop tools, configurations, and software/hardware preferences to build O-PAS systems which contain unique features not found yet in the market. They will also use these systems to test the performance and compatibility of these hardware/software components. With these features the system integrator will have a unique selling point and can differentiate itself from the competition.

question: What scope of test bed is necessary to demonstrate system integrator capabilities?
answer:
In order to demonstrate the capabilities of the system integrator, the test bed needs to show:

  • O-PAS component suppliers with which the system integrator has experience
  • O-PAS architecture techniques with which the system integrator has experience (e.g., system redundancy, system orchestration)
  • The integration of third-party products
  • Portability of software and hardware
  • Interchangeability and interoperability of hardware
  • Security features

All such questions define the scale of the test bed.

question: How do system integrators demonstrate that they embrace open, secure, and interoperable control systems?
answer: A system integrator can list all their experience with certified O-PAS products on their website. Having a test system to show end users their O-PAS integration capability is a reliable way for end users to show their commitment to the O-PAS Standard. Participating in Forums and panel discussions, doing presentations, and drafting white papers are other ways which also give great exposure to end users.

question: How do system integrators demonstrate vendor neutrality?
answer: System integrators can publish lists of O-PAS hardware and software suppliers with which they cooperate, and for which they have preferences. A test bed system is a good instrument to show vendor neutrality as this test bed can be built from components supplied by different vendors that the system integrator has relationships with. System integrators should make statements on their website or in communications, that preferences or suggestions from end users for specific O-PAS products, services, or vendors can be integrated into their commercial offering.

question: How do system integrators demonstrate previous project experience with multiple vendors?
answer: System integrators who have finished, to the satisfaction of the end user, an O-PAS project, can ask the end user for permission to write a “success story” or be a reference. Such success stories and references can be published on the system integrator’s website. Some end users may allow the system integrator to bring potential O-PAS end users to their production site to witness the O-PAS control system. They can also talk to the end user to hear their experience of having an O-PAS system and working with the system integrator.

question: Are system integrators going to support the completed systems?
answer: The role of the system integrator is to offer and build a complete O-PAS system. After completion of the project, it is one of the tasks of the system integrator to handover the system to a service provider and provide training. The system integrator may take on the role of service provider. The service provider’s contract with the end user will define the level of service coverage.

question: How could system integrators establish legal contracts with the end user and their hardware and software suppliers (total system performance, liability)?
answer: The legal contract for an O-PAS system could be like the existing terms and conditions for a traditional DCS or SCADA system. It is a mutual, written agreement between the end user and the system integrator. The system integrator will also have legal agreements with the hardware and software suppliers.

question: How do we demonstrate system security?
answer:
O-PAS components are secure-by-design. If a product is O-PAS certified, its components are tested against security standards. For an O-PAS system, it is up to the system integrator to show to the end user that when O-PAS certified products are used wherever applicable that the system is secure.

Certification of entire systems is outside the scope of the O-PAS Standard. An end user that chooses to have the system certified for security could seek cybersecurity certification from an independent organization.

question: How do system integrators take their offers to market?
answer: A system integrator should build their Go-To-Market (GTM) strategy for promoting O-PAS systems depending on their market strengths in specific industries, geographic region, specific process, etc. They can use multiple marketing channels (events, webinars, newsletter, etc.) to promote their capabilities in O-PAS systems to their targeted customer segments. They could prepare white papers highlighting advantages over traditional control systems (from their project experiences) with an O-PAS system.

question: Which industries should system integrators target?
answer: Different industries use different combinations of continuous and discrete control, and these are part of the O-PAS Standard scope. The initial focus of the standard is on continuous and hybrid manufacturing. Discrete manufacturing will be considered later due to the type of equipment used and the requirements of discrete operation.

question: How do system integrators demonstrate their competitive advantage?
answer: As with any platform or capability in a system integrator’s service profile, they will need to demonstrate the competitive advantage of the O-PAS Standard via client references, applicable training, certifications, and successful implementation examples. Supplier partnerships, supply chain linkage, and in-house test beds may also demonstrate strengths and advantages of the O-PAS Standard.

question: How do system integrators market their O-PAS system capabilities and benefits?
answer: System integrators should demonstrate that they know their customer’s applications and challenges. They need to align their presentations addressing these challenges along with quantifiable benefits of the O-PAS system.

question: How do system integrators market their cybersecurity capabilities?
answer: System integrators should use their current cybersecurity marketing techniques and processes, but with the addition of any specific capabilities and service offerings related to O-PAS security, as the O-PAS Standard embeds security by design above what is seen in the industry today.

question: How do system integrators demonstrate IT/Operational Technology (OT) integration?
answer: IT/OT convergence facilitates real-time data exchange between the OT-physical world to the IT world of business applications. Core elements are data and cybersecurity. O-PAS systems demonstrate this convergence with standard data information models and “secure-by-design” components. system integrator demonstrating O-PAS capabilities are by default ready to take the next steps of integrating O-PAS systems with business systems.

question: How do system integrators show experience with test beds, Proof of Concepts (PoCs)?
answer: Many O-PAS test beds and development systems now exist, belonging to suppliers and end users. Partnership with these system owners may provide meaningful experience and opportunities with these systems for marketing purposes. It would certainly be advantageous for a system integrator to have such a system of their own for both developing skills and demonstrating capabilities specific to O-PAS implementation.

question: Which trade shows should system integrators attend?
answer: System integrators should leverage their strengths in the marketplace (for example, in a specific industry, geography/region, or equipment) by participating in these events and marketing O‑PAS systems and their value and benefits, to attract customers.

question: Should system integrators focus on Greenfield or Brownfield projects?
answer: With O-PAS systems it is not an either/or proposition, as the standard is targeted for both project types. While there are typically many more Brownfield projects and opportunities in general, this may be the area in which to focus first. Brownfield projects may also provide more opportunities for end users to begin their O-PAS deployment in phased and varied manners. However, it is fully expected and anticipated that O-PAS systems will be implemented in Greenfield opportunities as well, so the choice of focus is valid for either, or both types of O-PAS projects.

question: How does the system integrator interface with the end user for the project that will be using an O-PAS system?
answer: In an O-PAS system project, the interface between the system integrator and the end user shifts from implementing a single-vendor solution to orchestrating a multi-vendor, interoperable ecosystem. While the foundational project lifecycle remains familiar, the system integrator must collaborate with the end user much earlier to define specific design philosophies and select O-PAS certified products. An important component of this interface is the direct involvement of end-user engineering resources throughout the integration process; this “hands-on” partnership ensures that the internal team gains the technical knowledge required to troubleshoot and maintain the system once the project team departs.

question: How does the system integrator build a team for the project?
answer: It depends on the type of contract. An integrated team of the end user and the system integrator can be beneficial for efficient execution of a project.

question: Will the system integrator be involved before and during Front End Engineering Design (FEED) activities?
answer: This is determined during the kick-off meeting. It is recommended for new O-PAS systems that the system integrator be involved as early as possible.

question: How will the system integrator interact with the end user?
answer: At the start of a project, clear lines of communication, roles, and responsibilities should be established between the end user and the system integrator.

question: What is different for turnkey O-PAS projects?
answer: The contract for O-PAS projects will have specific FAT/SAT testing criteria that may be different from criteria for traditional control systems. Testing criteria must be outlined by the end user or the EPC to ensure the right expectations on deliverables.

question: What is the role of the system integrator in determining the scope of the project?
answer: It is a similar effort to scoping control systems projects today. Early involvement of the system integrator in projects is important as it provides opportunities to optimize the project scope and schedule.

question: What happens in the case where there are multiple system integrators?
answer: One of the system integrators should be designated by the end user to oversee the complete project and be responsible for the interfaces between all of the subsystems and its overall performance.

question: What type of expert advice will the system integrator provide to end users on how to deliver greater value on their project?
answer: System integrator typically has knowledge of multiple projects, which will be the same for O-PAS systems. The system integrator also has access to multiple resources from past experience including multi-vendor and open standards/integration.

question: How is the FAT performed with O-PAS systems?
answer: For an integrated hardware/software FAT, the system integrator will test the full functionality of the system. This should be witnessed by the end user witnessed. Since O-PAS systems are built from multi-vendor components, the FAT may be at the system integrator’s facility. The O-PAS Standard is a new interface standard, and therefore, the data communication between components are what require the most rigorous testing. If the end user requires an interface to an existing DCS/SCADA system, or to modular equipment (e.g., skid) provided by another supplier, it may be time-saving to provide those components to be tested during the FAT rather than in the field.

question: What needs to happen at the completion of the project?
answer: The end user should witness the SAT prior to contract completion, making sure that the performance of the O-PAS system matches the contract specifications. The system integrator needs to provide the O-PAS products with all component vendor contacts, project files, and all supporting documentation to the end user. The system integrator should cooperate with the end user and service provider on the details of the O-PAS system design and provide training.

question: What is a Sample Checklist by project stage?
answer:
For the most part, this will follow the same stages as the conventional DCS/PLC project today. system integrator responsibilities will include:

  • Planning and design stage
    • Collaborating with the end user to understand their requirements and objectives for the O-PAS system, including any product or supplier preferences such as mutually developed approved vendor lists
    • Collaborating with the end user to define performance criteria for the system
    • Conducting a site survey and assessing the plant’s existing infrastructure to identify potential design constraints for the O-PAS system, including necessary interfaces
    • Developing the O-PAS system’s functional and detailed design, including hardware and software, networking, and cybersecurity requirements
    • Creating a detailed project specification that outlines timelines, milestones, budgets, and resources required for the project
  • Implementation stage
    • Procuring, installing, and configuring the hardware and software components for the O-PAS system; e.g., sensors, actuators, DCNs, HMI, and application and system management software, and network communication infrastructure, as defined in the detailed design
  • Integrating the O-PAS certified and non-certified components of the O-PAS system into a cohesive system that meets the end user’s requirements and design specifications
  • Perform testing of vendor subsystems
  • Conducting FAT and SAT to ensure that the integrated O-PAS system meets end-user defined performance and functionality requirements, and is ready for deployment
  • Developing Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for the O-PAS system’s operation and maintenance
  • Commissioning stage
    • Testing the O-PAS system’s functionality and performance in a live plant environment
    • Conducting training sessions for plant operators and service provider/maintenance staff on how to operate and maintain the O-PAS system, with emphasis on the differences from what they were used to with the traditional control system
    • Resolving and documenting any issues or bugs that arise during the commissioning process
  • Hand over to maintenance and support stage
    • Providing training and technical support to the end user’s service provider and operations teams as needed
    • Turn over appropriate as-built documentation
    • Act as ongoing advisor to the end user
    • Conducting periodic system audits (if so desired by the end user) and performance evaluations to ensure that the O-PAS system continues to meet the end user’s requirements and performance standards

question: Does the end user have a preferred service provider?
answer: Yes. In some cases, the end user may have a preferred service provider that they would like to work with during the Support Phase. The end user may have prior experience with a particular service provider or may have specific requirements that they believe the preferred service provider can fulfill effectively. The system integrator should take into consideration the preferences of the end user and work collaboratively to ensure a smooth transition and engagement with the preferred service provider, provided it aligns with the project’s contractual agreements and requirements. However, it is important for the system integrator to maintain impartiality and evaluate the capabilities and suitability of the preferred service provider to ensure they can deliver the required O-PAS support services efficiently and meet the project’s objectives.

question: What is the difference with the system integrator’s role in an O-PAS business ecosystem during the Support Phase?
answer:
In the context of the evolving business ecosystem created by the O-PAS Standard, the Support Phase becomes increasingly crucial for the system integrator due to the shift in roles and relationships among vendors, system integrators, and service providers.

The following list highlights the importance of the Support Phase in this context:

  • System knowledge and expertise The system integrator, having been involved in developing and implementing the O-PAS Standard, possesses in-depth knowledge and expertise about the system. During the Support Phase, this knowledge becomes invaluable in ensuring the multi-vendor components’ smooth operation, maintenance, and troubleshooting. The system integrator’s understanding of the system’s intricacies and interdependencies allows them to provide adequate support and minimize downtime.
  • Transition and handover With the potential involvement of different vendors, system integrators, and service providers in the O-PAS ecosystem, the Support Phase requires effective transition and handover processes. Similar to the initial system integrator, the system integrator plays a vital role in facilitating a smooth transition to subsequent service providers. They can provide necessary support, assistance, and training during and after the transition, ensuring that the new service provider understands the system’s nuances and can effectively take over the support responsibilities.
  • Holistic system perspective The system integrator, having been involved from the initial stages, has a holistic perspective of the O-PAS ecosystem. They understand how different components and functionalities interact and impact each other. During the Support Phase, this comprehensive understanding allows the system integrator to address system-level issues, optimize performance, and provide valuable insights to the service provider(s) for efficient operations.
  • Vendor coordination Effective coordination among different vendors becomes critical in a multi-vendor ecosystem. Having established relationships with various vendors, the system integrator can serve as a central point of contact and facilitate collaboration and communication between vendors and service providers. This coordination ensures timely resolutions and streamlined support processes, minimizing potential blame or delays in issue resolution.

Overall, the Support Phase of the system integrator’s role becomes essential in the O-PAS ecosystem as it ensures system continuity, minimizes disruptions, optimizes performance, and enables effective collaboration among vendors, system integrators, and service providers. The system integrator’s expertise, system knowledge, and coordination abilities contribute to a seamless support experience and enhance the overall success and satisfaction of the O-PAS implementation.

question: Does the system integrator have an advisory role in suggesting a preferred service provider based on previous experience?
answer:
Yes, the system integrator can suggest a preferred service provider based on their previous experience and knowledge of the service provider’s capabilities. If the system integrator has worked with a particular service provider in the past and had a positive experience regarding their expertise, reliability, and ability to provide effective support, they may recommend that service provider to the end user.

Suggesting a preferred service provider can be advantageous for several reasons:

  • Familiarity: The system integrator is already familiar with the preferred service provider’s capabilities, support processes, and their ability to handle similar systems This can help streamline the transition and reduce the learning curve for the service provider in taking over the support responsibilities.
  • Effective collaboration: If the system integrator and the preferred service provider have previously worked together on similar projects, they may have established communication channels, processes, and mutual understanding This can facilitate effective collaboration between the system integrator and the service provider during the Support Phase, leading to smoother operations and issue resolution.
  • Seamless knowledge transfer: The system integrator can leverage their existing knowledge and experience with the preferred service provider to ensure a seamless knowledge transfer process They can provide insights, guidance, and specific instructions to the service provider, allowing them to quickly understand the system and its unique requirements.
  • Trust and reliability: Based on previous experience, the system integrator has confidence in the preferred service provider’s ability to deliver quality support services This can help build trust between the end user and the service provider, knowing that the system integrator has vetted and recommended a reliable service provider.

However, it is important to note that the final decision regarding the selection of the service provider rests with the end user. The system integrator can provide recommendations based on their expertise and experience, but the end user may have their own preferences, requirements, or evaluation criteria for choosing a service provider. Ultimately, the end user should evaluate the system integrator’s suggestion and make an informed decision that aligns with their objectives and expectations.

question: How does the system integrator warranty the system?
answer:
The system integrator typically provides a warranty for the system as part of their responsibilities during the Support Phase. The specific details of the warranty, including its duration and coverage, are usually outlined in the contractual agreement between the system integrator and the end user.

Here are some common ways in which the system integrator warranties the system:

  • Defect resolution: The system integrator takes responsibility for resolving any defects or issues that arise in the system during the warranty period This includes addressing software bugs, configuration errors, or any other problems that affect the system’s functionality or performance.
  • Maintenance and updates: The system integrator may provide regular maintenance and updates to the system during the warranty period This ensures that the system remains up-to-date, secure, and compatible with any evolving technologies or requirements.
  • Technical support: The system integrator offers technical support to the end user during the warranty period This support can be in the form of a helpdesk, ticketing system, or dedicated support team that assists the client in troubleshooting issues, providing guidance, and answering questions related to the system.
  • SLAs: The system integrator may define specific SLAs that outline the expected response time, resolution time, and service availability during the warranty period These SLAs serve as benchmarks to ensure that the system integrator meets the agreed- upon service levels.
  • Extended warranty options: In some cases, the system integrator may offer extended warranty options beyond the standard warranty period These options provide additional coverage and support for an extended duration, typically at an additional cost.

It is important to note that the specific warranty terms and conditions can vary depending on the project, contractual agreements, and the system integrator’s policies. The warranty typically covers defects and issues that arise from the system integrator’s work, but it may have limitations or exclusions for factors beyond the system integrator’s control, such as end user’s modifications or third-party integrations. It is crucial for both the system integrator and the end user to have a clear understanding of the warranty terms to ensure effective support and maintenance of the system.

question: How will the contractual arrangements be handled?
answer:
During the Support Phase, the contractual arrangements between end users and system integrators are typically governed by a separate agreement or an extension of the initial contract, similar to what is done today.

Throughout the Support Phase, both parties refer to the support agreement as the guiding document for their interactions and to ensure that the system integrator fulfills its support obligations effectively. Clear communication, regular reporting, and ongoing collaboration are important to maintain a strong working relationship between the end user and the system integrator.

question: How will the service provider be trained?
answer:
During the Support Phase, the system integrator may be responsible for training the service provider to ensure they have the necessary skills and knowledge to effectively support and maintain the system.

The following list highlights the training process that typically takes place:

  1. Training plan development
  2. Training materials preparation
  3. Training delivery
  4. Hands-on practice
  5. Question & Answer (Q&A) and knowledge transfer
  6. Training evaluation and feedback
  7. Ongoing support and mentoring

The training process may vary depending on the complexity of the system, the service provider’s existing knowledge, and the specific requirements of the Support Phase. The system integrator’s goal is to empower the service provider with the skills and knowledge required for independent system support, ensuring a smooth transition of responsibilities and a successful Support Phase.

question: What responsibilities will remain with the system integrator?
answer:
During the Support Phase, even with a service provider, the O-PAS system integrator retains certain responsibilities to ensure the system’s overall success. Typically, the system integrator handles major enhancements or additions and warranty work.

It is important to note that the specific responsibilities retained by the system integrator can vary based on the contractual agreement between the parties, the complexity of the system, and the capabilities of the service provider. The goal is to establish a collaborative partnership where the system integrator and the service provider work together to ensure the ongoing success and stability of the system.

Overall responsibilities may include:

  • System oversight: The system integrator maintains an overarching responsibility for the system’s performance and functionality They monitor the system’s health, availability, and performance metrics to ensure it meets the agreed-upon service levels and remains in optimal condition.
  • Escalation point: The system integrator serves as an escalation point for complex issues or challenges that may arise during the Support Phase If the service provider encounters difficulties in resolving certain issues, they can escalate them to the system integrator for further assistance, guidance, or collaboration in finding solutions.
